planting.note: Plant container stock or rooted cuttings in spring on shaded, rocky slopes in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil with sharp drainage; this gorge shrub resents standing water at the root collar even though it demands high ambient humidity.

directions: Mountain fetterbush grows on the steep, boulder-strewn slopes and bluffs within the Chattooga, Jocassee, and Eastatoe gorge system, where constant waterfall-generated humidity and deep leaf litter keep its roots cool and moist. Unlike the evergreen Leucothoe fontanesiana of the same gorges, this species is deciduous, dropping its leaves after a brilliant orange-red fall display, and bears arching, one-sided racemes of small white urn-shaped flowers along bare stems before new growth emerges in spring. It is propagated almost exclusively by semi-hardwood cuttings taken from wild-collected or botanical-garden stock, since seed set and viability are low and inconsistent. Site it on a shaded, well-drained slope with reliably moist but never waterlogged soil to mimic its native rocky gorge habitat.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (Weakley)

planting.note: Plant divisions in early spring directly into consistently moist, humus-rich, acidic soil on a shaded slope; this variety establishes slowly and should not be allowed to dry out during its first two seasons.

directions: Harper's heartleaf is a large-leaved, spray-zone variety of mottled wild ginger restricted to moist slopes and streambanks within the Blue Ridge Escarpment gorges of South Carolina, North Carolina, and Georgia, where it grows within reach of waterfall mist. It differs from the nominate variety by its notably larger, more elongated, boldly mottled leaves and larger, deeper maroon urn-shaped flowers held at ground level. Named for early-twentieth-century botanist Francis Harper, who documented the escarpment gorge populations, it forms slow-spreading evergreen colonies under heavy rhododendron and hemlock canopy. Grow it as a rock-garden or woodland-trough specimen in humus-rich, perpetually damp, acidic soil, replicating the seep-fed slopes of its home gorges.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (Weakley)

planting.note: Sow fresh seed directly in moist, rich seep soil in fall and leave undisturbed outdoors; seed typically requires two winters of cold exposure to break double dormancy, and plants take several years to reach flowering size.

directions: Small-flowered bunchflower grows scattered through rich coves, seepage slopes, and streambanks within the Blue Ridge Escarpment gorges, favoring the constantly saturated, mineral-rich soils below cliff seeps. Its broad, pleated, lily-like basal leaves give rise in midsummer to a tall, loosely branched panicle of small, star-shaped, greenish-yellow flowers that are easily overlooked against the deep shade of the gorge canopy. Like other Veratrum, every part of the plant contains toxic steroidal alkaloids, so it should be sited away from grazing animals and curious pets. It is slow to propagate and rarely offered commercially, but a handful of native plant specialty growers and botanical garden seed programs maintain stock from wild-collected seed.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (Weakley)

planting.note: Tuck divisions into crevices of acidic rock or a humus-rich rock-garden pocket kept continually damp; this variety needs the steady seepage or spray moisture of its native cliffs and declines quickly if the root crown dries out.

directions: Rugel's alumroot occupies wet, acidic rock faces kept perpetually damp by waterfall spray in the Blue Ridge Escarpment gorges, including the cliffs around Whitewater Falls and the Horsepasture and Thompson River corridors, in contrast to the drier limestone cave-mouth sites favored by the nominate variety further north. Its rounded, shallowly lobed leaves form tight rosettes wedged into narrow rock crevices, and airy, branched sprays of small white flowers appear on wiry stems in early summer. The variety commemorates nineteenth-century botanical collector Ferdinand Rugel, who worked these exact gorges. It is a true cliff-dweller best grown wedged into a constantly moist rock crevice or tufa-style planting rather than ordinary garden soil.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (Weakley)

planting.note: Separate rooted mat fragments and press them firmly into damp, humus-rich soil or moss on a shaded rock face; keep the surface constantly wet until new growth knits together, since this species browns rapidly if it dries out.

directions: Twisted-hair spikemoss forms low, dense mats on wet, shaded rock faces and boulders within spray distance of waterfalls in the high-rainfall gorges of the Blue Ridge Escarpment, a narrow range centered on the mountains of North Carolina, South Carolina, and Georgia. Its tiny, scale-like leaves taper into the characteristic twisted, hair-fine tips that give the species its name, forming a soft green carpet over mossy stone. It requires essentially unbroken humidity and will dry, brown, and fail to recover if allowed to desiccate for more than brief periods, so it is best grown at the base of a shaded, continually dripping rock feature or in a misted terrarium-style planting rather than open garden soil. Availability is limited to a few native plant society sales and rock-garden specialty growers working with regional ecotypes.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (Weakley)
